set: the generated conformance suite, the same clips and windows for every detector

sample.statement: 467 clips measured and kept, of 3000 clips in the committed design. 8 were measured and excluded. The run order is the whole spine (152 rows that walk one axis at a time) followed by the cross product shuffled with the committed seed, so a partial run is a random sample of the cross product with every sweep complete. Every number in this file is from that sample and from nothing else.

table_universe: the windows every detector saw. ffmpeg's photosensitivity filter has its first second dropped, so window 0 of every clip is missing from its denominator, and leaving it in the others' denominators would compare them on different windows.

flashmap_over_all_windows_note: flashmap hides the whole failing one second period, which begins in the calm second before the flashing. Over all windows that shows as false positives, and it is the difference between the two tables here. Neither number is the flattering one to quote on its own.

operating_points.chosen_on: this conformance suite, by best F1, before any real clip is touched
operating_points.note: flashmap's own thresholds are not tuned on either set. They come from the spec text and are the same numbers the analyser ships with.

area_fraction_of_picture.why_this_axis: neither baseline has an area rule, so a small strobe that WCAG excuses should still move their numbers

red_mode.why_this_axis: neither baseline has a red rule. A luminance matched red flash is invisible to a relative luminance detector and visible to one that reads gamma encoded luma, so what they score here is an accident of their colour handling and not the red rule

flash_rate_hz.why_this_axis: neither baseline has a one second window, so three flashes in a second and three in ten seconds look the same to them

near_threshold.why_this_axis: the clips that sit within 15% of a limit, against the ones that do not

environment_when_written.ffmpeg: ffmpeg version 8.1.2 Copyright (c) 2000-2026 the FFmpeg developers

EA IRIS.why: the pinned image at eval/baselines/iris/ has never built, and building it here would have taken the shared machine for a long time: the shared colima VM had 6 containers from another project running on 4 CPUs and 7.7 GiB. CLAUDE.md forbids touching containers, images or volumes this project did not create, and the build is a vcpkg source build of the whole IRIS dependency tree on two jobs. Skipped rather than fought, as the lane brief asked.
EA IRIS.how_to_run_it_later: make iris-build, then make iris-run VIDEO=... OUT=...
EA IRIS.effect_on_this_table: no IRIS number appears anywhere in this repository. The cross-check of our ground truth against IRIS that EVAL_PLAN section 4 asks for has not happened, so the ground truth stands on the spec text alone.

Apple VideoFlashingReduction.why: it needs Xcode, and xcode-select reports '/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools', which is Command Line Tools only. It is also cut list item 4 in EVAL_PLAN section 6, so it was never part of the committed comparison.
Apple VideoFlashingReduction.effect_on_this_table: none, it was never in it

what_the_baselines_are.naive mean luminance differencing: one number per frame, the mean of the luma plane, thresholded on the change between frames. No area, no colour, no one second window, no linear light. eval/baselines/naive_luma_diff/run.py
what_the_baselines_are.ffmpeg photosensitivity filter: a mitigator, not a reporter: it rewrites frames it thinks are unsafe, so a flag is inferred from where its output differs from the unfiltered decode. Its first second is dropped. eval/baselines/ffmpeg_photosensitivity/run.py
what_the_baselines_are.not a safety claim: neither baseline is a safety tool and neither one's output is a conformance result. They are here to show what has to be added on top.
